edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ εἰκὸς ὅτι φήσουσι πρὸς ταῦτα ὅσιον εἶναι τὸν τὰ πάτρια φυλάττοντα καὶ μηδαμῶς ἀνόσιον, ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) τὰ ἑτέρων οὐ τηρεῖ· πάλιν τε αὖ τὸν νομισθέντα ἀνόσιον εἶναι παρὰ τοῖσδέ τισι μὴ εἶναι ἀνόσιον, ὅταν κατὰ τὰ πάτρια τὰ μὲν ἴδια σέβῃ τὰ δὲ παρὰ τοῖς ἐναντίους ἔχουσι νόμους προσπολεμῇ καὶ καταθοινᾶται. ταῦτα δὲ ὅρα εἰ μὴ πολλὴν ἐμφαίνει τὴν περὶ τοῦ δικαίου καὶ ὁσίου καὶ εὐσεβείας ταραχὴν, οὐ διαρθρουμένης οὐδὲ φύσιν τινὰ ἰδίαν ἐχούσης καὶ εὐσεβεῖς εἶναι χαρακτηριζούσης τοὺς τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτὴν πράττοντας. εἴπερ οὖν ἡ εὐσέβεια καὶ ἡ ὁσιότης καὶ ἡ δικαιοσύνη τῶν πρός τι ἐστὶν, ὡς τὸ αὐτὸ εἶναι ὅσιον καὶ ἀνόσιον παρὰ τὰς διαφόρους σχέσεις καὶ τοὺς νόμους, ὅρα εἰ μὴ καὶ ἡ σωφροσύνη τῶν πρός τι ἀκολούθως ἔσται καὶ ἡ ἀνδρεία καὶ ἡ φρόνησις καὶ ἡ ἐπιστήμη καὶ αἱ λοιπαὶ ἀρεταί· ὧν οὐδὲν ἂν εἴη ἀτοπώτερον. ἁπλούστερον μὲν οὖν καὶ κοινότερον ἱσταμένοις πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου ἐκκειμένας λέξεις αὐτάρκη τὰ εἰρημένα· ἐπεὶ δὲ νομίζομεν καὶ τῶν ἐξεταστικωτέρων τινὰς ἐντεύξεσθαι τῇδε τῇ γραφῇ, φέρε ὀλίγα τῶν βαθυτέρων παρακινδυνεύοντες ἐκθώμεθα, ἔχοντά τινα μυστικὴν καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον θεωρίαν, περὶ τοῦ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐπόπταις νενεμῆσθαι χωρία τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς· καὶ τῶν κατειλεγμένων ἀτόπων φέρε ὅση δύναμις καθαρὸν παραστήσωμεν τὸν λόγον.
thought_title: Holiness is not a matter of custom
pass_a_gloss: But it is likely (εἰκός) they will say in reply that the one guarding (φυλάττοντα) the ancestral things is holy (ὅσιον) and in no way unholy (ἀνόσιον), since he does not (also) keep (τηρεῖ) those of others; and again that the one considered unholy among certain people is not unholy, when according to the ancestral things he reveres (σέβῃ) his own, and wars against (προσπολεμῇ) and feasts upon (καταθοινᾶται) the things among those having contrary (ἐναντίους) laws. See whether these things do not display (ἐμφαίνει) much confusion (ταραχή) about the just (δίκαιον) and holy (ὅσιον) and piety (εὐσέβεια), (piety) not being articulated/defined (διαρθρουμένης) nor having some proper nature (φύσιν ἰδίαν) and characterising (χαρακτηριζούσης) as pious (εὐσεβεῖς) those who do the things according to it. If then piety and holiness (ὁσιότης) and justice (δικαιοσύνη) are of relatives (τῶν πρός τι), so that the same thing is holy and unholy according to different relations (σχέσεις) and laws, see whether also temperance (σωφροσύνη) will consequently (ἀκολούθως) be of relatives, and courage (ἀνδρεία) and prudence (φρόνησις) and knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) and the other virtues (ἀρεταί); than which nothing would be more absurd. For those standing more simply (ἁπλούστερον) and commonly (κοινότερον) against the set-out words of Celsus, what has been said is sufficient (αὐτάρκη); but since we think some of the more inquiring (ἐξεταστικωτέρων) will also meet (ἐντεύξεσθαι) this writing (γραφή), come, venturing (παρακινδυνεύοντες) let us set out a few of the deeper things, having a certain mystical (μυστικήν) and secret/unspeakable (ἀπόῤῥητον) contemplation (θεωρία), about regions (χωρία) of those on earth having been allotted from the beginning to different overseers; and come, as far as power allows (ὅση δύναμις), let us present (παραστήσωμεν) the account/teaching (λόγον) pure (καθαρόν) of the absurdities enumerated (κατειλεγμένων).

rejected: in no way unholy because he does not also keep those of others
choices.why: ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) ... οὐ τηρεῖ: 'in no way unholy because he does not also keep those of others' (could be read as the reason he is not unholy) changed to 'not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well'

pass_b_english: But they will probably say in reply that the man who keeps his ancestral customs is holy, and not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well; and again, that the man considered unholy by certain people is not unholy when, following his ancestral customs, he worships what is his own, and makes war on and feasts upon what is revered among those whose laws are the opposite of his.

But see whether this does not reveal great confusion about what is just and holy, and about piety, as though piety had no clear definition, nor any nature of its own that marks out as pious those who act in accordance with it. If, then, piety and holiness and justice belong among relative things, so that the same thing is holy and unholy according to different relations and laws, see whether temperance too will not consequently be relative, and courage, and prudence, and knowledge, and the rest of the virtues; and nothing could be more absurd than that.

Now, for those who take a simpler and more ordinary stand against the words of Celsus set out above, what has been said is enough. But since we think that some readers of a more searching kind will also come upon this writing, let us venture to set out a few of the deeper matters, which hold a certain mystical and secret insight, about the regions of the earth having been allotted from the beginning to different overseers; and let us, as far as we are able, present the teaching clear of the absurdities we have listed.
notes: ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) τὰ ἑτέρων οὐ τηρεῖ: καί is Koetschau's supplement and the double negative is awkward; read as 'he is not unholy on the ground that he does not also keep the customs of others', rendered 'not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well' so the English cannot be read as giving the reason he is not unholy. τὰ ... προσπολεμῇ καὶ καταθοινᾶται: 'makes war on and feasts upon' what others revere (e.g. eating animals that another people worships, as in 5.27); 'revered' is supplied from the contrast with τὰ μὲν ἴδια σέβῃ. τῶν πρός τι: the Aristotelian category of relatives, rendered 'relative things'. Temperance, courage and prudence, with justice already named beside piety, are the classical cardinal virtues; knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) is added to them. μυστικὴν καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον θεωρίαν rendered 'a certain mystical and secret insight' (θεωρία: contemplative insight into a deeper meaning). μὲν οὖν opening the third paragraph rendered 'Now', not 'For'. This chapter introduces Origen's reading of Deuteronomy 32:8-9 and Genesis 11 in 5.29; no Scripture is quoted here.
Open doubt (review): 5.28: ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) ... οὐ τηρεῖ has a double negative and depends on Koetschau's supplement. The translation gives the likely sense, and the note says so.

changes: ἐπεὶ μὴ (καὶ) ... οὐ τηρεῖ: 'in no way unholy because he does not also keep those of others' (could be read as the reason he is not unholy) changed to 'not unholy in any way for failing to keep the customs of others as well'
ἁπλούστερον μὲν οὖν: 'For those' changed to 'Now, for those' (μὲν οὖν is not causal)
μυστικὴν καὶ ἀπόῤῥητον θεωρίαν: 'contain a certain hidden and secret contemplation' (calque) changed to 'hold a certain mystical and secret insight'
